title: Silver in the sand
hookLine: a glint in the sand looks like silver and it's a shell: Shankara's first lesson on the knowing that frees
carry: jnana: knowing that undoes the i-and-this mix-up

cards: Late afternoon on a beach. Something flashes in the wet sand, and a kid runs for it, shouting that it's silver. It isn't.
It's the inside of a shell, catching the light. For a few seconds, though, the silver was completely real to that kid. The running was real.
The shout was real. Nothing in the sand changed when the mistake was seen. Only the seeing changed.
That little scene is a Vedanta teaching example, and Shankara reaches for it before he has commented on a single line of the Brahma Sutra. Last week was the Brahma Sutra with Ramanuja.

teach.b: In this tradition it also names a whole way: freedom that comes through knowing, rather than through doing more. Shankara's commentary opens with a preface before the first sutra.
He sets two things side by side: the one who knows, the I, and everything that can be known, the this. They are as opposed, he says, as darkness and light. Neither can be the other.
And yet everyone mixes them up, all the time, without trying. I am tall. I am tired.
I am going. This is mine. The knower takes on the features of the known, and the known borrows the life of the knower.
He calls the mix-up adhyasa, placing one thing on another, like silver placed on shell, or one moon seen as two by a tired eye. Then something bold: ordinary life runs on this mix-up.
Everyday ways of knowing, even the rules for ritual action, all work inside it. He isn't mocking daily life; he's describing where it stands.
And the Upanishads, he says, are studied to undo the mix-up, not by adding a new experience, but by knowing. That knowing is jnana.
And this is the heart of Advaita, non-dualism: for Shankara, the true self, the atman, is not other than Brahman, and only the mix-up hides it. Not every Vedanta teacher accepts this preface.
Ramanuja argues against it at length in his own commentary, and his followers read the same sutras another way. For the next few days, Shankara makes his case through the first four lines.

how: Students in Advaita Vedanta traditionally read Shankara's commentary on the Brahma Sutra with a teacher, often beginning with his preface on adhyasa before the first sutra.

games.q: you're Shankara, about to comment on the Brahma Sutra's first line. what do you write first?
o: a word-by-word grammar of the first line.
a preface on how the I and the this get mixed up.
a list of rituals to do before reading.
games.why: he opens with adhyasa, the mix-up of knower and known, because the whole inquiry is about undoing it.

practice: Notice one sensation, maybe tiredness, maybe warmth in the hands, and hear the sentence the mind makes about it: I am tired. Then, gently, say it another way inside: tiredness is being noticed.
Don't argue with either sentence; just feel the small difference between them, and if you pray, rest in that noticing as your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Jnana. Knowing, and the way of freedom through knowing. For Shankara, the knowing that undoes the mix-up of the I and the this.

orig.note: Sanskrit: knowing, knowledge; also the name of the way of freedom through knowing.

carryVoice: Your line: jnana, knowing that undoes the mix-up of the I and the this. Nothing in the sand changed; only the seeing did. See you tomorrow.
